clue.text: Chrysanthemum giving excitement to one or two

blocks.note: a fever is a state of nervous excitement
one or two means a small number, a few; 'to' simply adds it on

explanation.surface: A flower that thrills a person or two who receives it.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant was once classed in the genus Chrysanthemum, so the botanical name serves as a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Feverfew is a daisy-like herb formerly placed among chrysanthemums by botanists, still grouped with them in many gardening books.

clue.text: How Samson went through the mill at Gaza

definitions.text: How Samson went through the mill at Gaza

blocks.note: surface reading: suffered a hard time, the idiom for an ordeal
setter's reading: Milton's line about the blinded hero toiling at the mill with slaves

explanation.surface: Asking how the biblical strongman endured his suffering in captivity.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Samson Agonistes has Samson 'Eyeless in Gaza, at the mill with slaves'; the Philistines blinded him and set him to grind corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Samson's eyes were put out by the Philistines, so he worked the Gaza mill without sight, exactly as Milton phrased it.

clue.text: A pretext one can give to destroy

indicators.note: to give is to bend or yield, so the letters before it can be pushed out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Any excuse will serve as a reason to wreck something.
explanation.definitionFit: To extirpate is to root out completely and wipe out, from the Latin for pulling up by the stem.

clue.text: London dog was so white

blocks.note: surface reading: a dog from the British capital
setter's reading: Jack London's wolf-dog hero of the novel White Fang, toothed like his name

explanation.surface: A city dog described as pale-coated.
explanation.walkthrough: London is the American author Jack London, whose novel White Fang is about a wolf-dog; the dog was 'so' in having fangs.
explanation.definitionFit: Having prominent canine teeth describes Jack London's hero, a wolfish animal named after his pale teeth.

clue.text: Prayer Book assurance that there will be neither bang nor whimper

definitions.text: Prayer Book assurance that there will be neither bang nor whimper

blocks.note: surface reading: a promise in the Anglican liturgy, closing the Gloria
setter's reading: T. S. Eliot said the world ends 'not with a bang but a whimper', so with no ending at all there is neither

explanation.surface: A liturgical promise that nothing will finish dramatically or feebly.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's The Hollow Men ends 'This is the way the world ends / Not with a bang but a whimper'; the doxology in the Book of Common Prayer closes with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase closing the Gloria Patri in the Book of Common Prayer means for ever, eternally, so no ending of any kind.

clue.text: Gathered in folds in Scotland

blocks.note: surface reading: describing fabric pleated or tucked up
setter's reading: the Scots verb for tucking up a skirt, which also suggests the Highland garment with pleats

explanation.surface: Cloth bunched into pleats, Scottish style.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots verb for tucking up skirts gives the participle; the pleated Highland garment named from it makes the clue doubly apt.
explanation.definitionFit: To kilt is a Scottish verb meaning to tuck up or pleat material, so a kilted skirt has been gathered into folds.

clue.text: Buckle or hook in kind of suit

definitions.note: a diamond, and diamonds is a suit in cards

indicators.note: to buckle is to bend out of shape, so the following letters are twisted

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Instructions for fastening a suit with a buckle or hook.
explanation.walkthrough: Suit means a suit of cards: the answer is the famous Indian diamond in the British Crown Jewels, so it is a kind of diamond.
explanation.definitionFit: The Koh-i-noor is a celebrated diamond, and diamonds are one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards.

clue.text: Follower of 13th century philosophy, even if obscure

blocks.note: the informal short spelling of though
to mist is to blur or obscure

explanation.surface: A disciple of a medieval school of thought, even if that school is little known.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Aquinas (1225-74) gave his name to this school of thought.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thomist follows the teaching of Thomas Aquinas, the thirteenth-century Dominican theologian and philosopher.

clue.text: The best one can do, like Kipling's gentlemen-rankers?

blocks.note: first meaning: as in 'do one's utmost', a noun for maximum effort
second meaning: Kipling's poem calls them 'damned from here to Eternity', so they are the most damned

explanation.surface: Effort at its utmost, as shown by Kipling's ruined gentlemen serving as private soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's poem Gentlemen-Rankers, the well-born men in the ranks are 'Damned from here to Eternity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing your damnedest is an idiom for trying your utmost, and as a superlative adjective it means the most damned.

clue.text: Whipped and spread thin

blocks.note: first meaning: thrashed, or whisked like cream or eggs
second meaning: hammered out flat, as metal is by a smith

explanation.surface: Something whisked and then smoothed out, like cream on a cake.
explanation.definitionFit: The past participle covers both whisking or thrashing and hammering metal into thin sheets, as with gold leaf.

clue.text: Though unfinished, the Song of Solomon contains much

definitions.note: read as 'the Son of Solomon' once the last letter goes
a description of a large bottle rather than a noun

indicators.note: unfinished means the word that follows loses its final letter before it is read

blocks.note: first meaning: with its tail cut off this becomes the son of Solomon, the biblical king who succeeded him
second meaning: a very large wine bottle holding six ordinary bottles

explanation.surface: A remark that the biblical book, though left incomplete, is rich in content.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut the last letter from Song and you have 'the Son of Solomon', King Rehoboam of Judah; the giant champagne bottle sizes are named after biblical kings.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehoboam is an outsize wine bottle, equal to six standard bottles, so it certainly holds a great deal.

clue.text: Help to become Quaker

blocks.note: to be is to exist as, a shortened form of become
Quakers belong to the Religious Society of Friends

explanation.surface: Advice that joining the Quakers would help you.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers' formal name is the Religious Society of Friends, so any Quaker is a Friend; 'Help' is the verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To befriend someone is to act as their supporter and assist them, so it can stand for help as a verb.

clue.text: Ready to get married in blue creation

indicators.note: a creation is something newly made up, so the preceding letters are reshaped into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A bride ready for her wedding in a blue outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nubile traditionally describes a young woman of marriageable age, from the Latin verb meaning to take a husband.

clue.text: Is Lambeth part of this religion?

indicators.note: part of tells you the answer is a piece lifted from the run of letters in the words before it

blocks.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Asking whether Lambeth, home of the Archbishop of Canterbury, belongs to a non-Christian faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Lambeth Palace is the London residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury, so the question sounds absurd about this faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the monotheistic faith founded through the Prophet Muhammad, so it is precisely a religion.

clue.text: Can't bear to make a deduction on a silk hat

blocks.note: to infer is to conclude by reasoning
tile is old slang for a hat, especially a top hat

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot stand having to guess things about a top hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't bear' looks like intolerance; it means cannot produce offspring. 'On' places the first piece above the second in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: An infertile creature cannot conceive or produce young, so it is unable to bear children in the reproductive sense.

clue.text: What one member may make of the Rotary movement

definitions.text: What one member may make of the Rotary movement

blocks.clueFragment: What one member may make of the Rotary
blocks.note: surface reading: a member of the Rotary Club, the businessmen's association, and their view of it
setter's reading: a member is a limb, so this is a spin made on one leg, a turning movement

explanation.surface: One Rotary Club member's opinion of the whole Rotary organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rotary Club is an international service club for business people; 'member' is really a leg and 'Rotary movement' a spinning motion.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet a pirouette is a full spin of the body balanced on one foot or leg, a rotating movement.

clue.text: Unsuccessful batsman's claim to get a flier

blocks.note: a batsman out for nought has scored a duck, and might say he had one

explanation.surface: A batsman out for nothing ends up with a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero. The batsman's rueful 'I'd a duck' is what you say aloud; no separate indicator is printed, as the spoken claim signals it.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck of northern coasts, famous for its down, so it is a bird that flies.

clue.text: Quote for decorations

definitions.note: describes the formal statement accompanying an award, not the medal itself

blocks.note: first meaning: a passage quoted from a book or author
second meaning: the official commendation read out when a medal is awarded

explanation.surface: A quotation offered as ornament or embellishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Decorations here are military honours, not ornaments; each award comes with a written statement of the deed.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both a quoted passage and the formal mention of bravery that accompanies a gallantry award.

clue.text: Warning of something ridiculous -a forward guide

blocks.note: the golfer's shout to warn players ahead of an incoming ball
a sight is a person or thing that looks ridiculous; 'of' just joins

explanation.surface: An alert that something absurd is coming, then a guide pointing ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: FORE is what golfers shout; 'you look a sight' means you look ridiculous. A foresight is also the front sight on a gun barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means planning ahead, a guide to the future, and literally the front aiming sight on a rifle.

clue.text: Tack, or sometimes iron these

definitions.note: a description: these are sometimes called iron

blocks.note: first meaning: food, as in hardtack, a sailor's biscuit
second meaning: iron ... are a soldier's emergency food supply

explanation.surface: Choose between tacking a garment or pressing it with an iron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tack' and 'iron' look like sewing and laundry; tack is food and iron rations are emergency supplies carried by troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Fixed allowances of food issued to soldiers or sailors are their provisions, which old slang calls tack.

clue.text: Burnt a powder

blocks.note: taken as written
dust is fine powdery matter

explanation.surface: Someone describes a scorched powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Adust is an old literary adjective meaning scorched or dried up by heat, as of sunburnt land or parched complexion.

clue.text: Of the nervy sort -that is to say. one with a twitch

blocks.note: short for scilicet, Latin for namely
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
a tic is an involuntary muscular twitch

explanation.surface: Describing a jumpy sort of person, namely one with a nervous twitch.
explanation.walkthrough: SC, for scilicet, is the dictionary abbreviation for 'that is to say'. 'Nervy' points to a nerve, not to anxiety.
explanation.definitionFit: Sciatic describes the great nerve running down the back of the leg, so it relates to a particular nerve.

clue.text: A go-slow by the Musicians' Union?

definitions.text: A go-slow by the Musicians' Union?

blocks.note: surface reading: industrial action in which workers deliberately slow down
setter's reading: what musicians call a slow passage, marked by its Italian tempo direction

explanation.surface: Union members in the music business staging a work-to-rule.
explanation.walkthrough: A go-slow is a British form of industrial protest; the Musicians' Union is the British trade union for players.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian tempo marking means at a slow, leisurely pace, and names a slow movement in a piece of music.

clue.text: It can be made to retain images

definitions.text: It can be made to retain images

indicators.note: can be made says the following letters can be formed into something else

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Describing something that can be adapted to hold pictures, like film.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye holds images formed by the lens.
explanation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive lining of the eyeball where images are focused and captured for the brain.

clue.text: Subordinate gets order to miss game, perhaps

blocks.note: under means lower in rank, subordinate to
to bid is to command or order

explanation.surface: A junior employee is told to skip a match.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, game is a contract worth enough points to win a game; to underbid is to bid too low and so miss making game.
explanation.definitionFit: Underbidding at bridge means calling fewer tricks than the hand could make, which can cost the partnership a game bonus.

clue.text: Edmund's goose step, for example

blocks.note: a goose is a tailor's heavy smoothing iron
a sidestep is one kind of step, so the step is exemplified by its first part

explanation.surface: Someone called Edmund marching in the stiff-legged military style.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Ironside was an English king of 1016; the definition is his byname. The tailor's goose is an old pressing iron. The step-to-SIDE link is loose: a sidestep is a step.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund II of England was nicknamed Ironside for his valour against the Danes, so it is Edmund's epithet.

clue.text: Fish noises

blocks.note: first meaning: tropical sea fish named for the sounds they make
second meaning: low guttural sounds, as a pig makes

explanation.surface: Sounds made by fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun names both a family of warm-water fish that croak when caught and short snorting sounds like a pig's.

clue.text: This officer is young to be on the staff

blocks.note: first meaning: the most junior commissioned rank, once an infantry flag-bearer
second meaning: a flag flown from a flagstaff

explanation.surface: A junior officer, too young to serve on the general's staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' sounds like the headquarters staff of an army, but it is the pole a flag flies on.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a navy's lowest commissioned rank and a national flag flown at a ship's stern on its pole.

clue.text: Means of propulsion but not for a punt

definitions.text: Means of propulsion but not for a punt

blocks.clueFragment: Means of propulsion but not for a punt
blocks.note: surface reading: how to move a flat river boat, which is pushed along with a pole
setter's reading: propelling a rugby ball, where a punt is a different kick from the one that bounces off the ground

explanation.surface: A way of moving a boat that does not suit a punt on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt is both a pole-driven boat and a rugby kick from the hand; the answer is the kick where the ball touches the ground first.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby a drop-kick strikes the ball just as it bounces off the ground, unlike a punt kicked straight from the hands.
